title: The fire at Siddhashrama
hookLine: two boys stay awake six nights so a sacred fire can be finished
carry: guard the yajna, the sacred fire

lines: THE SIXTH DAY: A RAIN OF BLOOD.
cards: At Siddhashrama, Vishvamitra begins his sacrifice and takes a vow of silence; from now on he can't say a word. So the hermits tell the boys: for six days and six nights, you have to guard him.
Rama and Lakshmana stand watch, bows ready, and don't sleep. Five days pass. Nothing.
On the sixth, the altar fire suddenly flares up on its own. The sky goes dark. And out of the dark comes a roar, and a rain of blood.

teach.b: Maricha and Subahu have come, with their followers, to wreck the rite. Rama takes up the manava weapon, the one named for Manu, the first human, and fires it at Maricha's chest. It doesn't kill him.

teach.h: HURLED OVER THE SEA, STILL ALIVE.
teach.b: It hurls him a hundred yojanas, far out over the sea, where he falls, stunned but alive. Then the fire weapon for Subahu, who falls dead, and the wind weapon for the rest. The sacrifice is finished.
Vishvamitra, his vow complete, says: you've made the name of this place come true. Siddhashrama, the hermitage of accomplishment. Why does a whole week build toward guarding one fire?
Because the yajna, the fire offering, is worship as old as Hinduism's oldest scriptures, the Vedas. In the Vedas, Agni, the fire, carries what's offered to the gods.

Hindus still light that fire: a havan or homa at a housewarming, at a child's rites of passage, and at weddings, where the couple walks around the sacred fire. Rama spent six nights awake so one could be finished.
Hold onto Maricha. He's still out there, and he'll come back as a golden deer.
Now the week, from the top. A given word. A dawn verse.
A question asked before acting. Ahimsa first, force last. Mantras given to the ready, and the strength to call them back.

how: The yajna Rama guards is the fire offering at the heart of Vedic worship; Hindus still offer into a sacred fire in the havan or homa at housewarmings and rites of passage, and circle it at weddings. Ramayana tellings also mark Maricha's survival here, since he returns in the Aranya Kanda as the golden deer.

games.q: you're Rama. Maricha attacks the sacrifice. you hold the manava weapon. what do you do?
o: strike him so he's hurled far away, alive.
games.why: the manava hurls Maricha a hundred yojanas over the sea, senseless but alive. he'll be back, as the golden deer.

practice: Many Hindu homes light a small lamp, a diya, morning or evening, a small everyday flame offered to God. Light one if you can, or picture its flame.
Then sit as if you're on watch, not tense, just awake: eyes low, back long, breath even, noticing each sound arrive and pass the way the boys watched the dark for six nights.
If your attention wanders, come back to the flame without scolding yourself. If you pray, offer the sit itself.

wordCard.voice: The weapons. At Siddhashrama, Rama uses them for the first time: the manava hurls Maricha out to sea alive, and the yajna is completed.

carryVoice: Your line: guard the yajna, the sacred fire. Six nights awake, and the offering was finished. A week on the road, complete.
